Siena enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a 23-11 team that finished 13-7 in MAAC regular-season play, then won the MAAC Tournament title by beating Fairfield 76-61 on March 8, 2026 and Merrimack 64-54 on March 10, 2026. The Saints were listed at 23-11, 13-7 MAAC in Siena’s own postgame notes after the title game, and the MAAC championship release confirms Siena won the league tournament as the No. 3 seed. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/news/2026/3/11/mens-basketball-seventh-heaven.aspx))

From a traditional scouting lens, Siena is built around an old-school formula: veteran guard control, half-court execution, paint scoring, defensive rebounding, and late-clock toughness. The offense starts with point guard Justice Shoats organizing the game, but the primary volume scorer is Gavin Doty, who entered the MAAC final averaging 17.7 points and 7.0 rebounds while playing 36:38 per game. Shoats entered that same game averaging 4.4 assists, and Siena as a team ranked second in the MAAC in assist-to-turnover ratio at 1.31 while committing only 10.2 turnovers per game. Those numbers fit what shows up on film: Siena is not a random, freelance offense; it wants a controlled possession ending with a Doty drive/post mismatch, Shoats paint touch, or a kick-out to Brendan Coyle. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/sienasaints.com/documents/2026/3/10/MBB_Game_Notes_-_MAAC_Merrimack_3.10.26.pdf))

Specific offensive tendencies show up in game recaps. Against Manhattan on January 17, Siena recorded 22 assists, its highest total in six years, with Shoats, Doty, and others sharing creation duties in a 74-59 win. That is strong evidence of continuity offense with inside-out ball movement rather than pure isolation. Against Canisius on February 1, Siena produced a 34-12 edge in points in the paint while Francis Folefac had 14 points, nine rebounds, and five assists; that suggests a lot of elbow and low-post facilitation through the frontcourt. Against Niagara on January 30, Shoats had 25 points and six assists with zero turnovers in an 82-79 road win, a classic lead-guard game in which he controlled tempo and late possessions. Against Iona on February 5, Doty scored 25 with 13 rebounds and Folefac added 17 and 12, showing Siena can run offense through a scoring wing and a rim-running big in the same night. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/news/2026/1/17/mens-basketball-three-cheers.aspx))

Named actions are not always diagrammed in public recaps, but the results point to several recurring sets and play families. First, Siena clearly uses high ball-screen offense for Shoats, because his assist totals, low-turnover games, and paint production repeatedly drive efficient team shot profiles. Second, Siena uses post touches and duck-ins for its frontcourt: in the MAAC title game it won the paint 32-12 and in the Canisius road win it won the paint 34-12. Third, Siena leans on flare and kick-out threes for Brendan Coyle, who had four games with at least five threes entering the conference final; his seven-threes game against Manhattan on January 17 is the clearest example of the staff hunting movement shooting for him. Fourth, Siena will play through Doty as a mismatch scorer late; he had 13 games of 20 or more points entering the title game and scored 25 against both Iona and Fairfield in major February/March spots. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/news/2026/3/11/mens-basketball-seventh-heaven.aspx))

Defensively, Siena’s identity is much clearer and more consistent. This is a scoring-defense program first. On January 22 against Marist, Siena entered ranked 23rd nationally in scoring defense at 65.7 points allowed and then held Marist to 14 second-half points on 21% shooting in a 69-50 win. On January 11 against Mount St. Mary’s, Siena entered ranked 19th nationally in scoring defense at 65.1 and held the Mount to 29% overall, 22% from three, and held the starting backcourt to 1-for-21 from the field. In the MAAC final against Merrimack, Siena entered ranked 20th nationally in scoring defense at 66.0 and held the Warriors to 29.3% shooting, their second-lowest scoring output of the season, while recording 10 blocks. That profile says Siena is a compact help-defense team that protects the lane, contests without over-fouling when disciplined, and finishes possessions with rebounds. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/news/2026/1/23/mens-basketball-outfoxed.aspx))

The defensive philosophy also appears matchup-specific. Against Merrimack in the title game, Siena used Francis Folefac on MAAC Player and Rookie of the Year Kevair Kennedy and held him to 5-for-18 shooting after Kennedy had torched Siena for 32 points and 16-for-16 foul shooting in Merrimack’s 79-72 overtime win on February 20. That is a documented adjustment by Gerry McNamara’s staff: the first meeting got away because Kennedy lived at the line and Merrimack shot 11-for-25 from three; the rematch featured Folefac as a length matchup, only four Kennedy free-throw attempts, and a 10-block avalanche by Siena. That is not theory; it is game-to-game evidence of a coaching staff changing the coverage and primary defender. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/news/2026/2/20/mens-basketball-merrimack-edges-saints-in-overtime-heartbreaker.aspx))

McNamara’s coaching philosophy looks like former-guard pragmatism: defend first, trust experienced guards, shorten the rotation in big games, and ride what is working. The MAAC title game recap noted Siena used only seven players, and the AP/CBS game report noted Christian Jones was the only reserve McNamara used. In other words, when the stakes rose, McNamara cut the bench and relied on Doty, Shoats, Coyle, Folefac, Mulvey, Chandler, and one reserve. Another documented adjustment came on January 22 against Marist: after a grindy first half, Siena changed the texture of the game with a devastating 39-14 second half by winning points in the paint 22-4 and points off turnovers 12-0 in that half. On February 5 against Iona, Siena erased a double-digit deficit and won 79-72 with a 13-0 second-half burst, again showing a coach willing to alter matchups and ride the hot hand rather than force balance. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/news/2026/3/11/mens-basketball-seventh-heaven.aspx))

Late-game and clutch execution are legitimate strengths, even with a few notable failures. Siena closed the MAAC final by letting Merrimack cut the lead to 51-47 with 3:47 left, then Doty answered by scoring Siena’s next six points, including a dagger three with 2:19 left, to push it to 57-50. In the February 5 win over Iona, Siena came back from a double-digit hole and finished the game with a 13-0 second-half run. In the January 11 win at Mount St. Mary’s, Siena closed on a 16-3 run over the final 5:21, and Christian Jones hit a 30-foot shot-clock-beating three with 3:47 left. In the March 1 regular-season finale win over Rider, Siena used a 19-4 second-half run and got 17 of Brendan Coyle’s 20 points after halftime. The flip side: at Merrimack on February 20, Siena led late, got a clutch Isaiah Henderson corner three to go up 64-62 with 1:33 left, but could not get the final stop in regulation and lost 79-72 in overtime; that game revealed some vulnerability against elite foul-drawing guards and hostile-road officiating environments. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/news/2026/3/11/mens-basketball-seventh-heaven.aspx))

The key players start with Doty, the team’s closer and most dependable big-shot scorer. He entered the MAAC final at 17.7 points and 7.0 rebounds per game, with 13 20-point games and six double-doubles on the season. His standout moments are everywhere: 25 points and 13 rebounds vs. Iona on February 5, 25 points vs. Fairfield in the MAAC semifinal on March 8, 23 points in the MAAC title game on March 10, and 21 points with 16 in the second half vs. Marist on January 22. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/sienasaints.com/documents/2026/3/10/MBB_Game_Notes_-_MAAC_Merrimack_3.10.26.pdf))

Shoats is the floor general and emotional regulator. He entered the title game averaging 4.4 assists, had one 10-assist game on the season, and authored several high-leverage performances: 25 points, six assists, zero turnovers at Niagara on January 30; 22 points at Canisius on February 1; 26 points against Fairfield in the MAAC semifinal; and 18 points on 8-for-11 shooting with zero turnovers at Mount St. Mary’s on January 11. When Siena needs the offense organized, Shoats is the one flattening the floor and making the correct read. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/sienasaints.com/documents/2026/3/10/MBB_Game_Notes_-_MAAC_Merrimack_3.10.26.pdf))

Coyle is the specialist who changes geometry. He had four games with at least five made threes entering the MAAC final. His best tape is January 17 at Manhattan: 23 points, 10 rebounds, seven threes, and Siena’s season-high 13 made threes as a team. He also scored 17 of his 20 points in the second half against Rider on March 1. When Siena needs spacing and an off-ball movement shooter, Coyle is the answer. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/sienasaints.com/documents/2026/3/10/MBB_Game_Notes_-_MAAC_Merrimack_3.10.26.pdf))

Folefac is the x-factor big. He entered the title game shooting .537 from the field and averaging 1.2 blocks. His major moments include 17 points, 12 rebounds, and three blocks in the Iona win; 14 points, nine rebounds, and five assists at Canisius; and the defensive assignment on Kevair Kennedy in the MAAC final, where Kennedy was held to 5-for-18 shooting. Folefac gives Siena rim protection, a lob/paint target, and a switch piece against bigger guards. Antonio Chandler also matters as an efficiency forward; he posted a career-high 19 points on 9-for-10 shooting at Marist on February 15 and had eight 10-rebound games on the season leaderboard. Riley Mulvey’s value is interior rebounding and size; he had a career-high nine rebounds at Mount St. Mary’s. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/sienasaints.com/documents/2026/3/10/MBB_Game_Notes_-_MAAC_Merrimack_3.10.26.pdf))

The notable wins tell you Siena’s ceiling. The 64-54 MAAC title win over Merrimack showed they can choke off an elite mid-major offense with size and discipline. The 76-61 semifinal win over Fairfield showed shotmaking travel: Siena hit 9-of-17 from three, held Fairfield 14 points below its season average, and limited Braden Sparks to 1-of-6 from deep. The February 5 win over Iona showed comeback mettle against a rival. The 69-50 win over Marist showed this team can win ugly, and the 83-54 MAAC-opening blowout of Niagara on December 5 showed what happens when the bench gives real scoring punch. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/news/2026/3/11/mens-basketball-seventh-heaven.aspx))

The losses matter too. The February 20 overtime loss at Merrimack exposed issues against foul pressure and opponent star guards. The January 14 home loss to Sacred Heart, 86-80, exposed perimeter-coverage limitations: Siena entered that game ranked 14th nationally in scoring defense at 64.2, then gave up 15 made threes and a season-high point total. That result is the clearest blueprint for an NCAA opponent: spread Siena out, force multiple closeouts, and make them guard all five spots. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/news/2026/2/20/mens-basketball-merrimack-edges-saints-in-overtime-heartbreaker.aspx))

As for the head coach’s NCAA Tournament history, Gerry McNamara is in just his second season as Siena head coach, and this 2026 bid is his first NCAA Tournament appearance as a head coach. Siena’s March 10 championship recap states this is the program’s first actual NCAA Tournament appearance in 16 years and its first MAAC Championship Game win since 2010. There is no prior NCAA head-coaching round history for McNamara to list before 2026. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/news/2026/3/11/mens-basketball-seventh-heaven.aspx))

Bottom line: Siena is a classic upset-profile mid-major because it has a real closer in Doty, a composed point guard in Shoats, a movement shooter in Coyle, and a defense that has already held Marist to 50, Mount St. Mary’s to 50, Fairfield to 61, and Merrimack to 54. If the game is played in the 60s and Siena can keep the opponent off the foul line and off the offensive glass, the Saints are dangerous.

Siena enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a classic low-major auto-bid with a much stronger win-loss résumé than its national predictive profile. The most concrete public ranking signal I could verify is Siena’s NCAA NET trajectory and comparable ranking ecosystem. On WarrenNolan’s team page, Siena is listed at 23-11 overall and 13-7 in the MAAC, with a live RPI of 116 as of Sunday, March 15, 2026. That same WarrenNolan weekly history shows Siena’s NET improving from a preseason 287 to 109 by Week 20, while its ELO improved to 183 and RPI to 116. A separate NET-tracking page shows Siena’s team sheet with a likely current NET in the low 100s entering the tournament window, plus a quadrant profile of 0-1 in Q1, 0-0 in Q2, 2-6 in Q3, and 21-4 in Q4. The broad takeaway is that Siena won a lot, but did so against a very soft schedule, with almost no high-end résumé wins and very few chances to prove top-100 quality. Siena is confirmed as the MAAC automatic qualifier for the 2026 NCAA Tournament, and one bracket-related listing shows a March 19, 2026 neutral-court game against Duke, which is the kind of pairing consistent with a deep-underdog seed line. 

The schedule context is the single most important driver of Siena’s profile. WarrenNolan’s NET strength-of-schedule table places Siena 359th nationally in overall NET SOS and 338th in non-conference SOS. That is near the absolute bottom of Division I and explains why Siena’s record and conference title did not translate into an at-large caliber ranking profile. In practical terms, the Saints look like a team that handled business against weak and lower-middle competition but was not stress-tested in a way that predictive systems usually reward. This is the key divergence between résumé optics and underlying evaluation: a 23-11 conference champion sounds sturdier than a team with a NET around 109, ELO 183, and bottom-10 SOS. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-rank?team=Siena))

Because paywalled or bot-protected sources prevented direct extraction of Siena’s exact 2026 KenPom and ESPN BPI numbers, I cannot responsibly assign fake exact values. What the accessible data does show is that Siena’s predictive standing is materially weaker than its tournament status. WarrenNolan’s ELO rank of 183 and NET/RPI split strongly imply that Siena is not tracking like a top-100 efficiency team despite winning the league. The likely interpretation is that Siena sits outside the national efficiency conversation but above the typical 14-15 seed disaster profile because it did consistently bank wins in league play and closed the season on an upward NET arc from the high 180s into the low 100s. If KenPom is available behind subscription, Siena is almost certainly much closer to the 150-200 band than to the top 100, based on the combination of bottom-tier SOS and only modest NET/ELO standing. That is an inference from the available ranking cluster, not a directly retrieved KenPom figure. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-rank?team=Siena))

On style, the available game-level advanced data suggests Siena is neither a pure rock fight team nor a true tempo extremist. Individual game possessions from Sports-Reference commonly sit in the low-to-upper 60s: 60.8 in a January 4 win over Rider, 62.6 in a January 17 win over Manhattan, 64.6 in the January 19 win over Fairfield, 67.5 in the January 14 loss to Sacred Heart, 68.5 in the February 7 loss to Saint Peter’s, and 70.8 in the November 29 win over American. That pattern implies a roughly average or slightly below-average pace rather than a pressing, transition-heavy identity. Siena appears comfortable winning in both controlled half-court games and more offense-leaning MAAC possessions, but the data available does not support labeling them as especially fast. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/rider/men/2026-gamelogs-advanced.html?utm_source=openai))

The offensive identity looks more interesting than the national rankings would suggest. In several key wins, Siena posted highly efficient box-score profiles. Against Rider on March 1, Siena produced a .586 true shooting rate, .509 eFG%, .264 3-point attempt rate, .472 free-throw rate, 21.9% offensive rebound rate, 54.2% assist rate, and only a 9.7% turnover rate, good for a 116.9 offensive rating in that game. Against Saint Peter’s on February 22, Siena logged a .609 TS%, .512 eFG%, a very low .140 3PA rate, but a massive .791 free-throw rate and 34.8% offensive rebounding, leading to a 120.0 offensive rating. Earlier in the year, opponent-derived advanced logs show Siena reaching 121.7 offensive efficiency against Rider, 118.3 against Manhattan, 131.6 against Fairfield, and 131.1 against Niagara. Those game samples point to a team that can generate very efficient offense in-league without relying on huge three-point volume. Instead, Siena’s best offensive performances appear to come from shot quality, foul pressure, and selective ball security. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/boxscores/2026-03-01-14-siena.html?utm_source=openai))

That said, the defensive side appears much shakier and is probably the reason Siena’s predictive profile lags its record. In the same opponent-derived logs, Siena allowed 106.9 to Rider even in a win, 119.2 to Fairfield in a win, 127.5 to Sacred Heart in a loss, and 102.1 to Saint Peter’s in another loss. Even in the March 1 win over Rider, Siena’s game defensive rating was 93.8, which is solid for one night, but the broader accessible sample suggests defensive volatility rather than a stable shutdown unit. The eye-test narrative of “conference champion = well-balanced tournament team” is likely wrong here. Siena seems more like an offense-first, matchup-sensitive team whose defense can be stretched by competent shot-making and by teams that avoid empty possessions. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/boxscores/2026-03-01-14-siena.html?utm_source=openai))

Recent form is encouraging, though not dominant. Siena’s schedule/results page shows a late-February overtime loss at Merrimack on February 20, 2026, but the team sheet also shows wins over Saint Peter’s on March 1 and Rider on March 7, plus a neutral-site MAAC tournament win over Mount St. Mary’s on March 8 before the conference final. WarrenNolan’s NET history is especially telling: Siena rose from 188 in Weeks 16-17 to 194 in Week 18, then jumped to 188 in Week 19 and all the way to 109 by Week 20. That is a very large late-season move and indicates their closing stretch materially improved the profile, likely through a combination of wins and the inherent boost of conference tournament games. So the last-10 trend looks positive in directional terms even if exact last-10 adjusted efficiency splits were not publicly retrievable. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/siena/men/2026-schedule.html?utm_source=openai))

The clearest analytical synthesis is this: Siena is better than the caricature of a random 20-plus-win mid-major, but weaker than the conventional romance around a conference-tournament champion. Their résumé says “dangerous underdog with momentum”; their schedule-adjusted profile says “one of the weaker teams in the field.” The numbers that most diverge from conventional wisdom are the brutally low 359 NET SOS and the middling 183 ELO, both of which argue that Siena’s record overstates its national strength. But the game-level efficiency evidence complicates that by showing a team capable of real offensive punch: good eFG nights, very low turnover games, strong foul generation, and enough offensive rebounding to pressure smaller or softer opponents. If Siena is going to outperform seed expectations, it will probably be because its offense is more functional than the national ranking systems imply. If it gets buried early, it will be because the defense and schedule inflation finally collide with high-major talent. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/sos-net))
matchup-analyst:
Siena enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a defense-first, half-court MAAC champion that wins with physical drives, foul pressure, and a very concentrated top-five rotation rather than with pace or depth. The Saints averaged just 70.7 points per game, which ranked 355th nationally, but allowed only 65.0 per game; they also posted a positive rebounding margin (+2.8), a positive turnover margin (+0.7), and only 10.3 turnovers per game as a team. Their main offensive engines are Gavin Doty (17.9 ppg, 206-for-445 FG, 46.3%), Justice Shoats (13.2 ppg, 149 assists, 88 turnovers), and Francis Folefac (11.1 ppg, 51.9% FG), with Brendan Coyle functioning as the volume spacer despite a lower 33.6% FG. Antonio Chandler gives them efficient interior finishing at 64.1% FG in 29 games. In practice that means Siena prefers to let Doty and Shoats create the first advantage, then finish through Folefac/Chandler or kick to Coyle. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/_/id/2561))

Style of play: Siena is most comfortable in a grind game where it can live in the paint, get to the line, and keep the ball secure. The clearest examples are the Jan. 14 loss to Sacred Heart and the Jan. 19 win over Fairfield. Against Sacred Heart, Siena scored 48 paint points and shot enough twos and free throws to reach 80, but generated only 5 fast-break points and just 3 points off turnovers; Sacred Heart stretched the floor with three different players making at least four threes, and Siena lost 86-80. Against Fairfield on Jan. 19, Siena again leaned into paint pressure and efficiency, winning 85-77 even while Fairfield got 20 points from Brandon Benjamin on 10-for-11 shooting. The disruption formula is therefore specific: wall off Doty/Shoats drives, make Siena become a jump-shot volume team, and punish their help defense with shooting. Sacred Heart did exactly that: Anquan Hill had 22, Nyle Ralph-Beyer 21, and Mekhi Conner 15 on 5-for-8 from three. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/boxscore.aspx?id=18398&path=mbball))

Press and zone vulnerability: the clearest pressure-related evidence is that Siena’s worst ball-security games came when primary creators were forced to handle extra stress. Their team season high was 20 turnovers against American on Nov. 29, and Shoats had season highs of six turnovers against both American and Fairfield. Fairfield also turned Siena over enough in the Jan. 19 meeting to generate 22 points off turnovers, compared with only 8 for Siena. That is strong evidence that aggressive ball pressure can distort the Saints’ normal low-turnover profile. Zone is also a viable tactic because Siena is not a reliable perimeter-volume team: for the season they shot only 179-for-585 from three, or 30.6%. The championship win over Merrimack is instructive here: Siena still won 64-54, but did so with just 4 points off turnovers and 4 fast-break points, meaning the offense was largely a half-court, shot-making, rebound-and-defend affair rather than easy creation. If a bigger opponent can zone the lane, rebound, and avoid losing Coyle in movement, Siena can bog down. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

Preferred pace and how to force the opposite: Siena does not want a track meet. Their scoring average, low assist total (13.4 per game), and repeated low fast-break outputs show a team more comfortable in controlled possessions than in tempo. Examples: Siena had only 8 fast-break points in the 75-72 loss at Iona, 5 in the 86-80 loss to Sacred Heart, 2 in the 74-62 loss to Quinnipiac, 0 in the 79-72 OT loss at Merrimack, and 4 in the 64-54 MAAC title win over Merrimack. To force the opposite, an NCAA opponent should score early in the clock, pick up full court after makes, and turn Siena’s short bench into a conditioning problem. The rotation data matters: Doty averaged 36.7 minutes, Shoats 35.6, Coyle 30.2, and Folefac 27.7. When the game stays compressed, those minutes are manageable; when the game becomes end-to-end, Siena’s reliance on core guards becomes a liability. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

Size and athleticism mismatches by position: at point guard, Shoats is listed at 5-11, 180, so high-major teams with 6-3 to 6-5 lead guards can shoot over him or force switches; Sacred Heart’s backcourt shot over Siena for 10 made threes in that Jan. 14 game. At the wing, Doty is a real plus at 6-5 and can punish smaller 2-guards, but he is still more scorer than stopper; Fairfield’s Brandon Benjamin scored 20 on 10-for-11, suggesting Siena can be attacked by efficient slashers/wings. At the other wing, Coyle’s value is spacing, but physically he is not a rim-pressure wing; against Merrimack on Feb. 20 he shot 2-for-10, all from three, which shows how opponents can top-lock or chase him off rhythm. Up front, Folefac is productive but foul-prone at 90 fouls in 34 games, and Chandler is only 6-6 despite excellent efficiency. That creates a specific problem against true size. Quinnipiac’s 6-9/6-10 front line hurt Siena badly on Feb. 13, especially Spence Wewe’s 18 rebounds and Amarri Monroe’s 21 points. Siena won the MAAC title with Riley Mulvey starting and posting 11 points, 11 rebounds, and 5 blocks, but Mulvey had played only 25 games and averaged 17.2 minutes, so depth against size is still a real concern. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster))

Isolation vs team offense tendencies: Siena is much more creator-driven than pass-heavy. Team assists were only 13.4 per game, while Doty and Shoats alone took 840 of Siena’s 1,827 field-goal attempts, or 46.0% of all shots. Doty individually used 24.4% of team attempts; Shoats used 21.6%; Folefac added 14.1%; Coyle 14.7%. That concentration points to a primary-creator offense rather than egalitarian movement. The assist data supports that further: Shoats had 149 assists, but the team’s assist/turnover ratio was only 1.3, and in several stress games Siena’s assists were modest relative to possessions. In the Iona loss they had just 12 assists on 27 made baskets; in the title win over Merrimack they had 12 assists on 21 made baskets. This is not pure isolation every trip, but it is clearly an offense that leans on individual shot creation and direct ball-screen advantage more than on complex shared creation. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

Transition offense and defense frequency: Siena’s transition offense is low-frequency based on repeated box-score outputs. In the five evidence games above, Siena scored 8, 5, 2, 0, and 4 fast-break points respectively, for an average of 3.8 across those games. Even in wins, transition was rarely central. Defensively, their transition containment is more mixed: in the MAAC title they allowed Merrimack 11 fast-break points while winning because they dominated the paint 32-12 and rebounded; against Fairfield on Jan. 19 the opponent had 6 fast-break points and 22 points off turnovers, which is the cleaner model for attacking Siena—speed them up enough to get live-ball chances, not just early-clock misses. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/boxscore.aspx?id=18394&path=mbball))

Coaching adaptability: there is evidence Gerry McNamara’s staff adjusts, but mostly game-to-game rather than in a literal playoff “series” format, because college basketball does not use playoff series. The best concrete example is Merrimack. Siena lost at Merrimack 79-72 in overtime on Feb. 20 while getting only 3 bench points and 0 fast-break points, and with Shoats limited to 11 minutes. In the MAAC championship rematch on March 10, Siena changed the texture of the game: Mulvey started and delivered 11 points, 11 boards, and 5 blocks; Siena held Merrimack to 24 second-half points and won 64-54. Another adjustment marker appears in team record splits: Siena was 14-0 when leading at halftime but only 2-9 when trailing, which suggests the staff is excellent protecting scripted advantages but less proven digging out once an opponent establishes control. ([sienasaints.com](https://sienasaints.com/boxscore.aspx?id=18408&path=mbball))

Concrete gameplan: To beat Siena you must do four specific things. First, gap Shoats and Doty and make Siena prove it from three; the Saints shot only 30.6% from deep for the season. Second, pressure the ball without overhelping—Fairfield’s 22 points off turnovers and Siena’s season-high 20 turnovers vs American show the ball can be disrupted. Third, attack their frontcourt with size and offensive rebounding; Quinnipiac’s Spence Wewe grabbed 18 boards, and Chandler/Folefac are productive but not a big, deep power-conference front line. Fourth, force bench minutes and pace by making Doty and Shoats defend multiple actions every trip. If Siena can keep the game in the 60s and live at the line, it is dangerous.
